sections.heading: Fast, Straight Answers When the System Quits
body: Wichita asks a lot of a heating and cooling system. Summer afternoons run past 100 degrees, and winter cold snaps push a furnace through long, hard nights. Parts that were already worn tend to give out exactly then.
That is why we book same-day and next-day appointments. We are open Monday through Sunday, 8am to 5pm, and emergency calls are available.
When we get there, we find the failed part, explain what it is and lay out your options.

sections.heading: We Explain Before We Fix
body: A system that stops working is confusing, and it's easy to feel pushed into a decision. We slow that part down.

The technician finds the problem, explains what failed, and walks you through the options: repair the part, replace a larger component, or replace the system. You get the reasoning, not just a number.
If the fix is a small part, we don't sell you a whole new unit.

sections.heading: AC Repair
body: Most calls start the same way. The house is creeping past 80, the vents are blowing warm air, and the outdoor unit is humming or silent.

The cause is usually small and cheap next to a new system: a failed capacitor, a tired fan motor, a clogged drain line or a refrigerant problem. Heat is hard on all of them, which is why they fail on the worst days.
We diagnose it, tell you what failed, and get the cold air back. If a repair doesn't make sense, we say that too.

sections.heading: Furnace and Heating Repair
body: A furnace that won't light, blows cold air or cycles on and off is telling you something specific. Dirty filters, a bad igniter or flame sensor and a worn blower motor cause most of it.
We repair furnaces, boilers and heat pumps. Once we know what's failing, you decide whether to fix it, with a straight answer on what that repair will do for you.
Winter outages don't wait for a convenient day, and neither do we. Call early and we'll work you into the schedule.

sections.heading: When It's Time to Replace
body: Sometimes a repair only buys a few months. A system that keeps breaking, runs constantly or can't keep up has told you what it needs.

Two questions help: how old is the system, and how many repairs has it needed lately? An older unit that keeps failing costs more every season, while a newer one with one bad part is almost always worth fixing.

We install and replace air conditioning and heating systems, and we'll tell you whether yours is worth another repair before we sell you a new one. Financing is available through Enhancify, so a replacement doesn't have to land on you all at once.

sections.heading: What Usually Fails, and Why
body: Air conditioners fail in heat because heat is when they work hardest. Here is what fails most often:
list: **Capacitors.** A small part that gives the motors the jolt to start. It weakens with heat and age, then the fan or compressor won't start. It is one of the cheapest and most common failures.
**Fan and compressor motors.** Hours of Kansas heat wear bearings and windings until the motor stalls or quits.
**Low refrigerant.** A system doesn't use up refrigerant, so low levels mean a leak somewhere that needs finding, not just topping off.
**Clogged drain line.** Algae blocks the condensate drain and a safety switch shuts the system down.
**Frozen coil.** Restricted airflow, usually from a dirty filter, lets the coil ice over and stops cooling.
tail: A technician who finds the real cause fixes it once. One who guesses sends you a second bill.

sections.heading: Repair or Replace?
body: A repair is usually the right call when the system is fairly young and one part has failed. A new capacitor or motor on a system that otherwise runs well is money well spent.
Replacement starts to make sense when the system is old, keeps breaking, or can't keep the house cool even when every part works. Spending repeatedly on a system near the end of its life rarely pays.
We give you the numbers on both and let you choose. If you go with a new system, financing is available through Enhancify.

sections.heading: Not Sure It's the AC?
body: Before you call, a quick check can save you a visit:
list: Confirm the thermostat is set to cool, below the room temperature, with working batteries.
Check that the breaker for the outdoor unit and the indoor air handler hasn't tripped.
Look at your air filter. If it's packed with dust, replace it.
Check for ice on the refrigerant lines or the indoor coil. If you see ice, turn the system off and let it thaw before calling.
tail: If those don't fix it, give us a call. Tell us what you see and hear, and that helps us arrive with the right parts.

sections.heading: The House Won't Warm Up
body: It might be a furnace that never starts, one that blows cold air, or one that runs a few minutes and shuts off. Or the house is warm in one room and cold in the next.
Each is a symptom, and each points to a short list of causes. Knowing the cause is the difference between a quick repair and a repeat visit.

sections.heading: What Usually Goes Wrong With a Furnace
body: Most furnace calls come down to a few parts:
list: **Dirty or clogged filter.** Restricted airflow makes the furnace overheat and shut itself off. It is the easiest fix and the most common cause.
**Igniter or flame sensor.** If the burner lights and then goes out, a dirty flame sensor is a frequent cause. A cracked igniter means the burner never lights at all.
**Blower motor.** The motor that pushes warm air through your ducts wears out. When it fails you get heat in the furnace and none in the house.
**Thermostat.** A dead battery or bad setting can look like a failed furnace.
**Pilot or gas supply.** On older furnaces, a pilot light that won't stay lit or a closed gas valve stops the heat before it starts.
tail: A furnace repair should end with you knowing which part failed and why. That is how we work.
Tell us the symptom when you call, such as the burner clicking without lighting or the blower running with no warm air. It helps us bring the right parts to your door.

sections.heading: Safety Comes First
body: If you smell gas, leave the house and call the gas company or 911 from outside. Don't flip switches or use the phone inside.
If a carbon monoxide alarm goes off, get everyone out and call 911. Furnaces with a cracked heat exchanger can leak carbon monoxide, which is why an odd smell, soot or a yellow flame is worth a call.
Never run a furnace you suspect is unsafe. Call us once everyone is safe.
